table_title: What are the top 5 highest mountains on each continent, with their height in meters, country, and year of first recorded summit?
db_analog: SELECT continent, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY continent ORDER BY height_m DESC) AS rank, mountain, height_m, countries, year_of_first_summit FROM source_defined_continent_mountain_rankings QUALIFY rank <= 5 ORDER BY continent, rank
temporal_note: Wikipedia per-continent master ranking articles + per-mountain articles, accessed 2026-04-27 to 2026-04-28. Heights and per-continent top-5 rankings come from height-ordered Wikipedia sources: List of highest mountains on Earth (Asia); Andes (South America, including Peru's Huascarán per the article's stated heights); List of mountain peaks of North America; Caucasus Mountains (Europe); List of mountains in Africa (which explicitly applies a topographic-prominence > 500 m independent-mountain rule); Sentinel Range (Antarctica, raw elevation); List of highest mountains of New Guinea (Oceania, applies a height >=3750m + prominence >=500m ranked-list rule). First-summit years come from per-mountain Wikipedia pages where they exist. Five rows have 'unknown' as the Year of First Summit because Wikipedia does not record the first ascent: Cerro Bonete (S America #5), Pushkin Peak (Europe #5), Clinch/Corbet/Schoening Peaks (Antarctica #3-#5). Per-continent independent-mountain conventions vary by source: Africa explicitly applies prominence > 500 m; Oceania applies a height >=3750m + prominence >=500m ranking rule per the List of highest mountains of New Guinea master article (which excludes Sumantri / Ngga Pulu / East Carstensz Peak as subsidiary peaks); Antarctica uses raw elevation per the Sentinel Range article. The instance commits to each continent's source convention rather than imposing a single global rule.
_extraction_notes: Multi-source instance built from height-ordered Wikipedia rankings: 7 per-continent ranking/list pages plus the Seven Summits convention anchor plus 26 per-mountain entity/detail pages — 34 source URLs total. Per-mountain Wikipedia pages supply first-summit years and verify heights/countries; per-continent independent-mountain conventions vary by source and are documented in decision_log. Audit-driven repairs across three cycles (cycle 1: 4 BLOCKING; cycle 2: 2 BLOCKING + 1 hygiene; cycle 3: 1 BLOCKING from improved Wiki-family discovery pass): (1) South America top 5 corrected to include Peru's Huascarán (6768 m, 1932) — Llullaillaco drops out below Cerro Bonete (6759 m); (2) Africa switched to List of mountains in Africa (height-ordered with prominence > 500 m rule) — top 5 includes Mawenzi (5149, 1912) and Mount Speke (4890, 1906); Ras Dashen and Karisimbi dropped; (3) Oceania anchored to the List of highest mountains of New Guinea master article (cycle 3, replacing cycle 2's Puncak-Jaya-article-based listing). The New Guinea master applies an explicit height >=3750m + prominence >=500m ranked-list rule and excludes Sumantri/Ngga Pulu/East Carstensz Peak as subsidiary peaks. Cycle-3 Oceania top 5: Puncak Jaya (4884, 1962), Puncak Mandala (4760, 1959), Puncak Trikora (4730, 1913), Ngga Pilimsit (4717, 1962), Mount Yamin (4540, 2018). All five have known first-summit years; Sumantri/Ngga Pulu/East Carstensz are dropped. (4) Year of First Summit column type is `text` with `unknown` sentinel for the five rows where Wikipedia does not record the first ascent (Cerro Bonete, Pushkin Peak, Clinch/Corbet/Schoening Peaks); (5) operation_type is `projection` per UI validator (curation_ui/app.py line 589); (6) `db_analog` does not claim a global topographic-prominence rule — per-continent conventions are documented per-source. Antarctica retains the Sentinel Range article's raw-elevation ranking; Oceania uses the New Guinea ranked-list rule (cycle 3); Africa uses the prominence > 500 m rule (its source's own rule). Composite PK is (Continent, Rank). Result: 35 rows × 6 columns, 0 duplicate composite PKs, 5 'unknown' Year cells, 5 empty Country(ies) cells (Antarctica peaks; no sovereign nation).
